questions.q: A cell contains a Cu electrode in Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) and a Ni electrode in Ni(NO₃)₂(aq), joined by a salt bridge and by wires. While the cell operates, the reaction Cu(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ni(s) occurs; this reaction is thermodynamically unfavored. Which classification of the cell, with its justification, is correct?
options: Galvanic, because it has two different metal electrodes joined by a salt bridge
Galvanic, because electrons flow through the wires from one electrode to the other
Electrolytic, because both of its half-cells contain solutions of dissolved electrolytes
Electrolytic, because the unfavored reaction is driven by an outside power supply
optionWhy: A student who classifies a cell by its components picks this. The same two half-cells can form a galvanic or an electrolytic cell; what decides is whether the reaction that occurs is favored or unfavored.
A student who thinks electron flow shows that a cell is galvanic picks this. Electrons flow through the external circuit in electrolytic cells too, pushed by the power supply.

A student who takes 'electrolytic' to mean 'containing electrolytes' picks this. The classification is right but the reason is not: galvanic cells contain electrolyte solutions too. The cell is electrolytic because its reaction is unfavored and must be driven.

Galvanic cells use thermodynamically favored reactions; electrolytic cells use unfavored reactions driven by external electrical energy. Since the unfavored reaction occurs, the wires must connect the cell to a power supply.
questions.explain: Galvanic cells use thermodynamically favored reactions; electrolytic cells use unfavored reactions driven by external electrical energy. Since the unfavored reaction occurs, the wires must connect the cell to a power supply.

questions.q: The reaction Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) is thermodynamically favored. In the cell shown, a power supply drives electrons through the external circuit in the directions of the arrows. Which statement describes what happens at the Zn electrode while the power supply operates?
options: Zn²⁺ ions are reduced, so zinc metal builds up on the electrode
Zn atoms are oxidized and leave the electrode as Zn²⁺ ions
Zn²⁺ ions are reduced, so the electrode becomes smaller
Cu²⁺ ions that arrive through the salt bridge plate copper onto it
optionWhy: The arrows show electrons being pushed into the Zn electrode, so reduction occurs there: Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s). The power supply drives the unfavored reverse of the galvanic reaction, and the Zn electrode gains mass.

A student who thinks the favored reaction occurs whatever power supply is connected picks this. The power supply pushes electrons into the Zn electrode, so the half-reaction there is the reverse of the favored one: Zn²⁺ is reduced.
A student who links reduction with a decrease in size picks this. Reduction of Zn²⁺ deposits zinc metal on the electrode, so it grows and its mass increases.

A student who thinks Cu²⁺ ions travel through the salt bridge to the other electrode picks this. The salt bridge carries K⁺ and NO₃⁻; the ions reduced at the Zn electrode are the Zn²⁺ ions in its own solution.
questions.explain: The arrows show electrons being pushed into the Zn electrode, so reduction occurs there: Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s). The power supply drives the unfavored reverse of the galvanic reaction, and the Zn electrode gains mass.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell built from a Zn electrode in Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) and a Cu electrode in Cu(NO₃)₂(aq), the zinc electrode loses mass and the copper electrode gains mass as the cell operates. Which half-reaction occurs at the anode?
options: Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s)
Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻
Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Cu(s)
optionWhy: A student who thinks reduction occurs where the mass is reduced picks this. Reduction of Zn²⁺ would deposit zinc and increase the electrode's mass; the zinc electrode loses mass because zinc is oxidized.
The zinc electrode loses mass because zinc atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as Zn²⁺ ions. This oxidation occurs at the anode.

A student who thinks oxidation occurs at the electrode that gains mass picks this. Oxidizing copper would remove copper from the electrode; the copper electrode gains mass because Cu²⁺ is reduced there.
A student who thinks cations are produced at the cathode, and so consumed at the anode, picks this. Cu²⁺ is reduced at the cathode; the anode is where oxidation occurs, here of zinc.
questions.explain: The zinc electrode loses mass because zinc atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as Zn²⁺ ions. This oxidation occurs at the anode.
questions.working: The zinc electrode loses mass, so zinc atoms are leaving it as Zn²⁺ ions: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻. This is an oxidation (loss of electrons), and oxidation occurs at the anode. (At the cathode, Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Cu(s), which is why the copper electrode gains mass.)

questions.q: A student will build a galvanic cell at 25°C from two of the standard half-cells whose reduction potentials are listed in the table. Which two half-cells give the cell with the largest standard cell potential?
options: Cu and Al half-cells
Ag and Cu half-cells
Al and Mg half-cells
Ag and Mg half-cells
optionWhy: A student who multiplies each E° by its coefficient in the balanced equation picks this: 3(0.34) + 2(1.66) = 4.34 V looks largest. Without multiplying, this cell gives 0.34 − (−1.66) = +2.00 V, less than Ag/Mg.
A student who adds the tabulated reduction potentials picks the two most positive values: 0.80 + 0.34 = 1.14 V. The anode's potential is subtracted, so this cell gives only 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V.
A student who thinks more negative potentials release more energy picks the two most negative values. This pair gives only −1.66 − (−2.37) = +0.71 V.

E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is largest when the half-reaction with the most positive E° (Ag⁺/Ag, +0.80 V) is paired with the one with the most negative E° (Mg²⁺/Mg, −2.37 V): E°cell = 0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. No other pair exceeds this (for example, Cu/Mg gives +2.71 V and Ag/Al gives +2.46 V).
questions.explain: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode is largest when the half-reaction with the most positive E° (Ag⁺/Ag, +0.80 V) is paired with the one with the most negative E° (Mg²⁺/Mg, −2.37 V): E°cell = 0.80 − (−2.37) = +3.17 V. No other pair exceeds this (for example, Cu/Mg gives +2.71 V and Ag/Al gives +2.46 V).

questions.q: The diagram shows a galvanic cell at 25°C made from a standard Ag⁺/Ag half-cell (E° = +0.80 V for Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag) and a standard half-cell of an unknown metal, M, in M(NO₃)₂(aq). The arrows show the direction of electron flow, and the voltmeter shows the cell potential. What is E° for M²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → M(s)?
optionWhy: Electrons flow out of M, so M is the anode and Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode. 1.05 V = 0.80 V − E°(M²⁺/M), giving E°(M²⁺/M) = −0.25 V.
A student who thinks electrons flow toward the anode, and so takes M²⁺ as the species reduced, picks this: 1.05 = E°(M) − 0.80 gives +1.85 V. Electrons leave the anode, so M is oxidized.

A student who takes the voltmeter reading as the unknown half-cell's potential, made negative because M is oxidized, picks this. The reading is the difference between the two half-cell potentials, and the Ag⁺/Ag half-cell is at +0.80 V, not 0 V.
A student who doubles the Ag⁺/Ag potential because two Ag⁺ ions are reduced per M atom picks this: 1.05 = 2(0.80) − E°(M) gives +0.55 V. E° is not multiplied by coefficients.
questions.explain: Electrons flow out of M, so M is the anode and Ag⁺ is reduced at the cathode. 1.05 V = 0.80 V − E°(M²⁺/M), giving E°(M²⁺/M) = −0.25 V.
questions.working: Electrons leave the M electrode, so M is oxidized (anode) and Ag⁺ is reduced (cathode). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode: 1.05 V = 0.80 V − E°(M²⁺/M), so E°(M²⁺/M) = 0.80 V − 1.05 V = −0.25 V.

questions.q: The particulate diagrams represent the two half-cells of a galvanic cell before and after the cell operates for a short time. Each diagram shows part of an electrode and the solution next to it; water molecules and spectator ions are not shown. Based on the diagrams, how many electrons moved through the wire between the two electrodes during this time?
optionWhy: A student who takes the electrons transferred to be the number shown in one tabulated half-reaction, Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, picks this. That is the number gained by one Ag⁺ ion; six Ag⁺ ions are reduced in the diagrams, so 6 electrons are transferred.

Two Cr atoms leave the electrode as Cr³⁺ ions, each losing 3 electrons, so 2 × 3 = 6 electrons are released. Six Ag⁺ ions become Ag atoms, each gaining 1 electron, which accounts for the same 6 electrons.

A student who adds the electrons in the two half-reactions, 3 for Cr → Cr³⁺ + 3 e⁻ and 1 for Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, picks this. The electrons lost in the oxidation are the same electrons gained in the reduction, and here 2 Cr atoms lose 6 electrons in total.

A student who counts one electron for each particle that reacts picks this: 2 Cr atoms plus 6 Ag⁺ ions. Each Cr atom loses 3 electrons, so the 2 Cr atoms release 6 electrons, the same 6 that the six Ag⁺ ions gain.
questions.explain: Two Cr atoms leave the electrode as Cr³⁺ ions, each losing 3 electrons, so 2 × 3 = 6 electrons are released. Six Ag⁺ ions become Ag atoms, each gaining 1 electron, which accounts for the same 6 electrons.
questions.working: Cr half-cell: the electrode goes from 5 to 3 Cr atoms and the solution from 1 to 3 Cr³⁺ ions, so 2 Cr atoms are oxidized, Cr → Cr³⁺ + 3 e⁻, releasing 2 × 3 = 6 electrons. Ag half-cell: the solution goes from 7 to 1 Ag⁺ ions and the electrode from 2 to 8 Ag atoms, so 6 Ag⁺ ions are reduced, Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, gaining 6 × 1 = 6 electrons. Electrons transferred = 6.

questions.q: The standard reduction potentials at 25°C are +0.80 V for Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s) and −0.14 V for Sn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Sn(s). What is E° for the reaction 2 Ag(s) + Sn²⁺(aq) → 2 Ag⁺(aq) + Sn(s)?
optionWhy: As written, Sn²⁺ is reduced and Ag is oxidized, so E° = −0.14 V − (+0.80 V) = −0.94 V. The coefficient 2 does not change the potential of the Ag⁺/Ag half-reaction, and the negative sign shows the reaction as written is thermodynamically unfavored.

A student who multiplies the potential of the Ag⁺/Ag half-reaction by its coefficient picks this: −0.14 − 2(0.80). A standard reduction potential does not change when a half-reaction is multiplied, so E° = −0.14 − 0.80 = −0.94 V.

A student who adds the two reduction potentials as they appear in the table picks this: 0.80 + (−0.14). Ag is oxidized in this reaction, so its reduction potential is subtracted: −0.14 − 0.80 = −0.94 V.

A student who always subtracts the less positive reduction potential from the more positive one picks this: 0.80 − (−0.14). That is E° for the reverse reaction, in which Sn is oxidized; here Ag is oxidized and Sn²⁺ is reduced, so E° = −0.94 V.
questions.explain: As written, Sn²⁺ is reduced and Ag is oxidized, so E° = −0.14 V − (+0.80 V) = −0.94 V. The coefficient 2 does not change the potential of the Ag⁺/Ag half-reaction, and the negative sign shows the reaction as written is thermodynamically unfavored.
questions.working: In the equation as written, Sn²⁺ gains electrons (reduction) and Ag loses electrons (oxidation). E° = E°(reduction half-reaction) − E°(oxidation half-reaction), both as reduction potentials = −0.14 V − (+0.80 V) = −0.94 V. The potential of Ag⁺/Ag is not multiplied by 2. questions.q: A student measures the potentials of four cells at 25°C, each based on Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), with the concentrations shown in the table. Which claim is supported by the data?
options: E increases as the total concentration of ions in the two solutions increases
E depends on [Cu²⁺], the reactant ion's concentration, and not on [Zn²⁺]
E is greatest when both solutions are at the standard concentration of 1.0 M
E depends on the ratio of [Zn²⁺] to [Cu²⁺], and not on either concentration alone
optionWhy: A student who thinks more ions give a higher potential picks this. Cells 1 and 4 have very different total ion concentrations but the same potential, and cell 3 has fewer ions than cell 1 but a higher potential.
A student who thinks only the reactant ion's concentration matters picks this. Cells 1 and 3 have the same [Cu²⁺] but different potentials, so [Zn²⁺] affects E.
A student who thinks standard conditions give the largest potential picks this. Cell 3, with [Zn²⁺] = 0.10 M, has a higher potential (1.13 V) than cell 1 (1.10 V).

Cells 1 and 4 have the same ratio, [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1, and the same potential, although cell 4 is ten times more dilute. A larger ratio (cell 2, ratio 10) gives a lower potential and a smaller ratio (cell 3, ratio 0.1) a higher one, as expected as Q changes.
questions.explain: Cells 1 and 4 have the same ratio, [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] = 1, and the same potential, although cell 4 is ten times more dilute. A larger ratio (cell 2, ratio 10) gives a lower potential and a smaller ratio (cell 3, ratio 0.1) a higher one, as expected as Q changes.

questions.q: The graph shows how the potential, E, of a galvanic cell at 25°C depends on log Q for the cell reaction. Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: The cell reaction is at equilibrium when Q = 1
Both forward and reverse reactions stop when E falls to 0 V
The cell reaction is at equilibrium when Q = 1 × 10¹⁰
The cell potential would be below E° if Q were less than 1
optionWhy: A student who thinks standard conditions are equilibrium conditions picks this. At Q = 1 (log Q = 0) the graph shows E = E° ≈ 0.30 V, not zero, so the reaction is not at equilibrium.

A student who thinks reactions stop at equilibrium picks this. Where the line reaches E = 0 the cell is at equilibrium: the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so there is no net current.
The potential falls to zero at log Q = 10. E = 0 means there is no driving force: the reaction is at equilibrium, so K = 1 × 10¹⁰.
A student who thinks any departure from standard conditions lowers the potential picks this. The line rises toward smaller log Q, so for Q < 1 (log Q < 0) E would be greater than E°.
questions.explain: The potential falls to zero at log Q = 10. E = 0 means there is no driving force: the reaction is at equilibrium, so K = 1 × 10¹⁰.
questions.working: E = 0 where the line crosses the horizontal axis, at log Q = 10. The cell has no driving force there, so the reaction is at equilibrium: Q = K = 1 × 10¹⁰. At log Q = 0 (Q = 1), E = E° ≈ 0.30 V; for log Q < 0 the line would lie above 0.30 V.

questions.q: A galvanic cell based on Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) is operating at 25°C. Solid Cu(NO₃)₂ is dissolved in the copper half-cell, increasing [Cu²⁺], and the measured cell potential increases. Which explanation of the increase is correct?
options: The cell's equilibrium shifts toward products, as Le Châtelier's principle predicts
More ions are present in solution, so more charge carriers raise the potential
E° for the cell increases, because the reactant ion is now more concentrated
Q decreases, so the cell is farther from equilibrium, and its driving force is greater
optionWhy: A student who treats the operating cell as an equilibrium system picks this. A cell with a nonzero potential is not at equilibrium, so equilibrium arguments do not apply; the increase is explained by Q moving farther from K.
A student who thinks the potential grows with the total number of ions picks this. The potential depends on Q, a ratio; adding Zn²⁺ ions instead would also add ions but would lower the potential.
A student who confuses E with E° picks this. E° refers to standard conditions and does not change; the measured potential E increases because Q decreases.
Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] falls when [Cu²⁺] increases, moving the cell farther from equilibrium (Q = K). The cell potential measures this driving force, so it increases.
questions.explain: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺] falls when [Cu²⁺] increases, moving the cell farther from equilibrium (Q = K). The cell potential measures this driving force, so it increases.

questions.q: The diagram shows a concentration cell at 25°C. In which direction do electrons flow through the external circuit, and why?
options: From right to left, because electrons move away from the more concentrated Cu²⁺ solution
No electrons flow, because both electrodes are made of the same metal
No electrons flow, because the cell's potential is equal to its E° value, which is zero
From left to right, because this brings the two Cu²⁺ concentrations closer together
optionWhy: A student who expects electrons to move from high to low concentration, as in diffusion, picks this. That direction would make the concentrations more different; electrons flow from the dilute half-cell (anode) to the concentrated one (cathode).

A student who thinks identical electrodes give no potential picks this. E° = 0 for a concentration cell, but Q ≠ 1 here, so the cell has a potential and electrons flow until the concentrations are equal.
A student who thinks a cell's potential always equals E° picks this. E° = 0, but with unequal concentrations Q = 0.010 ≠ 1, so E = −(RT/2F) ln Q is positive.

The cell moves toward equilibrium, equal concentrations. Cu is oxidized in the dilute left half-cell (adding Cu²⁺) and Cu²⁺ is reduced in the concentrated right half-cell (removing Cu²⁺), so electrons flow from left to right.
questions.explain: The cell moves toward equilibrium, equal concentrations. Cu is oxidized in the dilute left half-cell (adding Cu²⁺) and Cu²⁺ is reduced in the concentrated right half-cell (removing Cu²⁺), so electrons flow from left to right.

questions.q: A student electroplates nickel onto a cathode from NiSO₄(aq) and lowers the current partway through the experiment. The graph shows the current in the cell during the experiment. What is the total mass of nickel deposited on the cathode? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.)
optionWhy: The charge is found for each period of constant current: (1.50 A)(400 s) + (0.50 A)(800 s) = 1000 C, which is 0.01036 mol of electrons. Each Ni²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons, so 0.005182 mol of Ni, 0.304 g, is deposited.
A student who thinks one mole of electrons deposits one mole of any metal picks this, taking 0.01036 mol of Ni. Each Ni²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons, so 0.005182 mol of Ni is deposited.
A student who multiplies the 0.005182 mol by the molar mass of NiSO₄, 154.75 g/mol, picks this. Only nickel is deposited on the cathode, so the molar mass of Ni, 58.69 g/mol, is used.

A student who multiplies the starting current by the total time picks this: (1.50 A)(1200 s) = 1800 C. The current was 1.50 A for only 400 s and 0.50 A for the remaining 800 s, so the charge is 600 C + 400 C = 1000 C.
questions.explain: The charge is found for each period of constant current: (1.50 A)(400 s) + (0.50 A)(800 s) = 1000 C, which is 0.01036 mol of electrons. Each Ni²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons, so 0.005182 mol of Ni, 0.304 g, is deposited.
questions.working: From the graph, the current is 1.50 A for 400 s and then 0.50 A for 800 s. q = (1.50 A)(400 s) + (0.50 A)(800 s) = 600 C + 400 C = 1000 C. Moles of electrons = 1000 C ÷ 96,485 C/mol = 0.01036 mol. Ni²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Ni(s), so moles of Ni = 0.005182 mol, and mass = 0.005182 mol × 58.69 g/mol = 0.304 g.

questions.q: In three experiments, the same quantity of charge is passed through a solution containing a different metal ion, and the metal deposited at the cathode is weighed. The results are shown in the table. Which claim is supported by the data?
options: Moles of metal deposited are directly proportional to the ion's charge
Moles of metal deposited are equal for the three ions, as the charge passed is equal
Moles of metal deposited are inversely proportional to the ion's charge
Mass of metal deposited is fixed by the charge passed, whichever ion is used
optionWhy: A student who thinks an ion with a larger charge gives more metal per mole of electrons picks this. The moles deposited fall from 0.0100 (Ag⁺) to 0.00500 (Cu²⁺) to 0.00334 (Au³⁺) as the charge of the ion rises.
A student who thinks the same charge deposits the same number of moles of any metal picks this. The masses correspond to 0.0100 mol, 0.00500 mol and 0.00334 mol, which are not equal.
Dividing each mass by the molar mass gives 0.0100 mol of Ag, 0.00500 mol of Cu and 0.00334 mol of Au: in the ratio 1 : 1/2 : 1/3 for ions of charge 1+, 2+ and 3+.
A student who thinks a given charge deposits a given mass of any metal picks this. The three masses, 1.08 g, 0.318 g and 0.657 g, are different although the charge passed is the same.
questions.explain: Dividing each mass by the molar mass gives 0.0100 mol of Ag, 0.00500 mol of Cu and 0.00334 mol of Au: in the ratio 1 : 1/2 : 1/3 for ions of charge 1+, 2+ and 3+.

questions.q: Two electrolytic cells are connected to one power supply as shown in the diagram, and a current passes for a fixed time. Metal is deposited at the cathode of each cell. Which statement correctly compares the amount of metal deposited in cell 2 with the amount deposited in cell 1?
options: Cell 2 deposits the same number of moles, as the same charge passes through it
Cell 2 deposits twice as many moles of metal, as an Ag⁺ ion gains half as many electrons
Cell 2 deposits half as many moles of metal, as each Ag⁺ ion has half the charge
Cell 2 deposits fewer moles of metal, as some current is used up in cell 1
optionWhy: A student who thinks the same charge deposits the same number of moles of any metal picks this. The same charge does pass, but each Cu²⁺ ion needs two electrons and each Ag⁺ ion needs one.

The cells are in series, so the same charge passes through each. Each Cu²⁺ ion gains two electrons and each Ag⁺ ion gains one, so the same moles of electrons deposit twice as many moles of Ag as of Cu.

A student who thinks an ion with a larger charge gives more metal per mole of electrons picks this. An ion with a smaller charge needs fewer electrons, so a given charge deposits more moles of Ag, not fewer.

A student who thinks current is used up as it passes through each cell picks this. Charge is conserved: the same current passes through both cells, and cell 2 deposits more moles because each Ag⁺ ion needs one electron.
questions.explain: The cells are in series, so the same charge passes through each. Each Cu²⁺ ion gains two electrons and each Ag⁺ ion gains one, so the same moles of electrons deposit twice as many moles of Ag as of Cu.

questions.q: A student electroplates copper onto a cathode from CuSO₄(aq) at constant current and records the mass of the cathode during the experiment. The results are shown in the graph. What is the current in the cell? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.)
optionWhy: A student who thinks one mole of electrons deposits one mole of any metal picks this, using 0.01888 mol of electrons. Each Cu²⁺ ion gains two electrons, so the charge and the current are twice as large.

A student who reads the height of the final point, 21.20 g, as the mass deposited picks this. The vertical axis shows the total mass of the cathode; the copper deposited is the change in mass, 1.20 g.
The cathode gains 1.20 g (0.01888 mol of Cu) in 800 s. Two electrons are needed per Cu²⁺ ion, so 0.03777 mol of electrons (3644 C) passes, and I = 3644 C ÷ 800 s = 4.55 A.
A student who uses the molar mass of CuSO₄ (159.61 g/mol) for the mass gained picks this. The cathode gains copper metal, so the moles deposited are 1.20 g ÷ 63.55 g/mol.
questions.explain: The cathode gains 1.20 g (0.01888 mol of Cu) in 800 s. Two electrons are needed per Cu²⁺ ion, so 0.03777 mol of electrons (3644 C) passes, and I = 3644 C ÷ 800 s = 4.55 A.
questions.working: From the graph, the cathode gains 21.20 g − 20.00 g = 1.20 g in 800 s. Moles of Cu = 1.20 g ÷ 63.55 g/mol = 0.01888 mol. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles of electrons = 0.03777 mol. q = (0.03777 mol)(96,485 C/mol) = 3644 C. I = q/t = 3644 C ÷ 800 s = 4.55 A.

questions.q: A student electroplates zinc onto a cathode from ZnSO₄(aq). During the experiment the mass of the cathode increases by 0.327 g. What quantity of charge passed through the cell? (F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.)
optionWhy: A student who thinks one mole of electrons deposits one mole of any metal picks this, taking 0.00500 mol of electrons. Each Zn²⁺ ion needs 2 electrons, so 0.0100 mol of electrons, 965 C, passed.

A student who thinks a 2+ ion gives twice as much metal per mole of electrons picks this, dividing the moles of Zn by 2 to get 0.00250 mol of electrons. The moles of Zn are multiplied by 2, because each Zn²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons.
A student who divides the mass gained by the molar mass of ZnSO₄, 161.44 g/mol, picks this. Only zinc is deposited on the cathode, so the mass is divided by the molar mass of Zn, 65.38 g/mol.
0.327 g of Zn is 0.00500 mol. Each Zn²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons, so 0.0100 mol of electrons passed, and q = 0.0100 mol × 96,485 C/mol = 965 C.
questions.explain: 0.327 g of Zn is 0.00500 mol. Each Zn²⁺ ion gains 2 electrons, so 0.0100 mol of electrons passed, and q = 0.0100 mol × 96,485 C/mol = 965 C.
questions.working: Moles of Zn deposited = 0.327 g ÷ 65.38 g/mol = 0.00500 mol. Zn²⁺(aq) + 2 e⁻ → Zn(s), so moles of electrons = 2 × 0.00500 mol = 0.0100 mol. q = 0.0100 mol × 96,485 C/mol = 965 C.

questions.q: In an electrolytic cell, a copper anode with an initial mass of 25.00 g and a copper cathode dip into CuSO₄(aq). A constant current of 1.930 A passes through the cell for 2000 s. What is the mass of the anode at the end of this time? (Molar mass of Cu = 63.55 g/mol; F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻.)
optionWhy: A student who thinks one mole of electrons reacts with one mole of any metal picks this, removing 0.04001 mol of Cu (2.54 g). Two electrons are released for each Cu atom oxidized, so 0.02000 mol (1.27 g) is removed.

A student who thinks the anode only completes the circuit, and that the copper deposited comes only from ions already in the solution, picks this. The copper anode is oxidized, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, and loses mass.
A student who places the deposition of metal at the anode picks this, adding 1.27 g. Cu²⁺ ions are reduced at the cathode, which gains mass; copper is oxidized at the anode, which loses mass.
3860 C is 0.04001 mol of electrons. Copper atoms of the anode are oxidized, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so 0.02000 mol of Cu (1.27 g) is removed and 25.00 g − 1.27 g = 23.73 g remains.
questions.explain: 3860 C is 0.04001 mol of electrons. Copper atoms of the anode are oxidized, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so 0.02000 mol of Cu (1.27 g) is removed and 25.00 g − 1.27 g = 23.73 g remains.
questions.working: q = (1.930 A)(2000 s) = 3860 C. Moles of electrons = 3860 C ÷ 96,485 C/mol = 0.04001 mol. At the copper anode, Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻, so 0.02000 mol of Cu is oxidized: 0.02000 mol × 63.55 g/mol = 1.27 g removed. Mass of anode = 25.00 g − 1.27 g = 23.73 g.

questions.q: A student electroplates copper onto a metal cathode from 1.0 M CuSO₄(aq), using a copper anode. A constant current of 0.50 A passes for 20 minutes, and the student measures the increase in the mass of the cathode. The student repeats the experiment with one modification, keeping the current at 0.50 A. Which modification is expected to double the increase in the mass of the cathode?
options: Doubling the length of time the current passes
Doubling the concentration of the CuSO₄(aq) solution
Doubling the area of the cathode in the solution used
Doubling the voltage setting on the power supply
optionWhy: At a constant current, q = I × t, so doubling the time doubles the charge, the moles of electrons and the moles of copper deposited.
A student who thinks a more concentrated solution deposits more metal picks this. The current and the time are unchanged, so the same charge passes and the same mass of copper is deposited.
A student who thinks a larger electrode gains more mass picks this. The same charge passes, so the same mass of copper is deposited, as a thinner layer over a larger area.
A student who thinks the applied voltage sets the amount deposited picks this. With the current held at 0.50 A for the same time, the charge and the mass deposited are unchanged.
questions.explain: At a constant current, q = I × t, so doubling the time doubles the charge, the moles of electrons and the moles of copper deposited.
